Agents of Chaos: Unpacking the Actions of Border Patrol Agents Across the US

In early January 2025, a gardener named Ernesto Campos was pulled over by Border Patrol agents in the city of Bakersfield, California.

Video footage shows one agent threatening to break Campos’ car window as they believed he was transporting an undocumented individual.

Campos filmed the agents, who he said slashed his tyres before arresting him and a passenger.

Ten months later, two of the agents visible in footage recorded by Campos were filmed in Chicago as Border Patrol agents descended on the city for what was dubbed “Operation Midway Blitz”.

One was seen grabbing a man by the throat before slamming him to the ground with help from other agents.

The other was seen punching a man in the face before pulling his gun on protesters in a Chicago suburb.

A federal judge in Illinois said in November that the use of force by federal agents in Chicago – including the use of tear gas and other less lethal munitions on multiple occasions – “shocks the conscience”.

Bellingcat has worked with our partners at Evident Media and CalMatters to analyse over 85 hours of social media and bodycam footage, as well as court documents and incident reports, to try to unpack the actions of Border Patrol agents across the country.

We observed over 25 agents who appeared in more than one city, either by recognising their faces or matching badge numbers that were visible on their vests or arm patches.

Many were seen alongside former Border Patrol Commander at Large, Gregory Bovino, on at least one occasion.

This story focused on the actions of five agents whom Bellingcat was able to identify and who appear to have repeatedly used force in at least two, but often more, locations.

The footage analysed appears to show a steady escalation of violence and confrontational incidents as 2025 progressed, culminating in widespread use-of-force incidents in Chicago and Minneapolis.

Two people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol agents, respectively, in early 2026.

Agents Timothy Donahue and Georgy Simeon were filmed by Ernesto Campos in Bakersfield.

Donahue was later pictured pointing his gun at citizens just outside Chicago after a traffic incident.

Donahue stated in his incident report that his car was rammed by an activist.

Illinois federal judge Sara Ellis’ opinion also described that Donahue’s car was rammed by an activist.

Donahue’s report made no mention of punching a man in the face or unholstering his weapon.

Simeon was filmed slamming a man to the ground after grabbing him by the throat.

Donahue was also spotted in social media footage in Los Angeles in June last year pushing a citizen who was blocking his vehicle.

Donahue was also spotted in social media footage in Los Angeles in June last year grabbing a man on an immigration raid inside a car wash.

The Chicago publication Unraveled Press previously reported that Donahue was the owner of a social media account that made seemingly racist and sexist posts.

Bellingcat and others checked this account and found that an old profile picture showed an image of Donahue.

Bodycam footage from outside a detention centre near Chicago showed Donahue tackle a journalist from Unraveled without apparent warning.

Footage from Donahue’s own bodycam on Oct. 3 appears to show him compiling an incident report with ChatGPT.

Judge Ellis wrote that using ChatGPT to write reports “undermines their credibility and may explain the inaccuracy of some reports filed by CBP officers”.

Bellingcat could not determine if Donahue used ChatGPT to compile the Oct. 31 incident report in which he did not mention he punched a man and unholstered his gun.

Our reporting partners CalMatters emailed and called Donahue prior to publication.

The email to Donahue received no response.

Donahue answered his cellphone but said, “never, ever call my cellphone again,” and hung up.

Simeon did not respond to emailed questions prior to publication.

Calls to a number listed under Simeon’s name went unanswered.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions posed about the actions of Donahue and Simeon detailed in this report or the agency’s use-of-force policies.

DHS did not respond to questions about whether it was permissible for agents to use generative AI platforms like ChatGPT to compile incident reports.

Kristopher Hewson, a supervisory agent based out of Bovino’s El Centro sector, was seen on bodycam footage in Chicago spraying an individual with oleoresin capsicum (OC), also known as pepper spray, from what appears to be just a few inches away.

Hewson said in his incident report that the individual had been resisting arrest.

Hewson stated in his incident report that he deployed the pepper spray from two feet away.

The bodycam footage showed the canister beside the individual’s head right after a burst of spray can be heard.

In bodycam footage from Chicago, a man said that the person Hewson pepper-sprayed was his son, who was just 15 years old.

An incident report showed the individual’s date of birth.

Hewson can be heard shouting “get back or you will be gassed” at a group of protesters immediately before deploying tear gas towards them.

As he throws the canister, a person can be heard shouting, “You’re not de-escalating shit, bro”.

Hewson stated in his incident report that he gave a warning that CS gas was coming.

A temporary restraining order on Oct. 9 prevented agents from using chemical agents on protesters and journalists unless there was an imminent threat of physical danger to federal forces.

That order was lifted in March 2026.

The order was still in force during the incidents detailed in this story.

Hewson was seen in Minneapolis in early 2026 alongside Bovino.

Hewson was captured on footage marching towards and tackling a Target employee, a teenage US citizen, who was directing insults at agents.

A melee ensued at the front door of the Target store before two people were handcuffed and taken away by agents.

Hewson’s C-29 number was visible as he led one of the men away.

Both of those arrested were later released.

In a preliminary injunction hearing in Chicago, Hewson stated (pages 183 and 184) that protesters have the right to shout and even swear at officers as long as they aren’t impeding their ability to carry out their work.

Hewson also said during questioning that tear gas “doesn’t harm people” (page 189).

Multiple individuals impacted by the release of gas and chemical irritants in Chicago stated otherwise in incidents detailed in Judge Ellis’ ruling.

When reached on the phone by CalMatters, Hewson said he could not comment.

Hewson was present and visible in footage when ex-Border Patrol Commander at Large Bovino appeared to push and manhandle a protester who crossed his path on Nicollet Avenue in Minneapolis.

Two officers based out of El Paso bearing the ID numbers EZ-2 and EZ-17 were beside Bovino and Hewson that day.

Both officers were wearing vests of the Border Patrol Tactical Division (BORTAC).

The CBP describes BORTAC as a specialised unit with a selection process “designed to mirror aspects of the US Special Operations Forces’ selection courses”.

Bellingcat and Evident Media previously reported that EZ-17 fired less lethal munitions at protesters from close range a day after Renee Good was shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis.

EZ-17 was accompanied during that incident by EZ-2.

EZ-2 sprayed a chemical irritant in the face of a man who appeared to have thrown a snowball at him.

EZ-2 was also seen throwing two female protesters to the ground outside Roosevelt High School in Minneapolis on Jan. 7.

EZ-17 and EZ-2 were present in Chicago.

EZ-17 was seen passing a tear gas canister to Bovino at an incident in Chicago’s Little Village neighbourhood on Oct. 23.

Bellingcat corroborated these identifications using similar techniques.

Bodycam footage from EZ-2 showed him looking at his phone.

When reached by phone by CalMatters reporters, Vazquez said that he could not comment.

Sveum hung up immediately after CalMatters’ reporter introduced himself.

DHS did not respond to questions posed about the actions of Vazquez or Sveum detailed in this report or the agency’s use-of-force policies.

Bovino himself appeared to instigate confrontations with people, such as in Chicago, when he can be seen throwing a man to the ground before agents pounce on him.

Bovino stated during his Illinois deposition that he did not think such actions represented a use-of-force incident.

Five Shots in Five Minutes: Analysing One Federal Agent’s Use of Less-Lethal Launcher in Minneapolis

The fatal shooting of Renee Nicole Good by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis on Jan. 7 sparked nationwide protests.

An elite Border Patrol officer, masked but identifiable through the uniform number patch EZ-17, was captured on camera firing his B&T GL06 40mm less-lethal launcher at protesters five times in five minutes.

EZ-17 fired the launcher while travelling down a street adjacent to where Good was killed.

Experts told Bellingcat the agent’s use of the less-lethal launcher was “punitive” and “questionable at best”.

Four of the shots appeared to be aimed directly at protesters’ faces at close range.

A fifth shot was fired from a distance towards a crowd after tear gas had already been deployed.

A sixth shot, captured at another location on the same day, shows EZ-17 firing a shot from the same launcher at someone at head-level.

In footage captured by independent news outlet Mercado Media, EZ-17 is seen inside the crime scene tape perimeter, standing near Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, with eight 40mm munitions on his belt.

These included three sponge-nose impact rounds.

These included five cylindrical munitions that can be filled with different payloads and chemical irritants.

“BLAST” in blue text is visible on one munition.

“BLAST” in blue text indicates a “Muzzle Blast” munition with a CS gas fill.

At least three additional 40mm munitions are visible in EZ-17’s plate carrier.

Another video by independent news network Status Coup News showed uninterrupted footage capturing five shots from the time the agent exited the crime scene perimeter at 5:02 to when he left in a truck with other agents at 9:23.

The back of EZ-17’s vest shows that he belongs to CBP’s Border Patrol Tactical Unit (BORTAC).

Members of BORTAC have regularly accompanied Bovino as he leads Trump’s immigration raids.

EZ-17 and EZ-2 have continued to accompany Bovino on raids in Minnesota in subsequent days.

EZ-17 was also spotted alongside Bovino at an incident in Illinois.

A CBP agent in front of EZ-17 in Illinois appeared to shoot a protester at close range.

The man slowly walks closer to the agents, saying that he has been maced.

EZ-17 pushes the man, then aims at the man’s face and fires.

The seals that keep the chemical irritant inside the 40mm canister before it is fired can be seen hitting the man in this shot.

An unmarked white CBP truck turns off the street and tries to drive down an alley after the third shot.

Protesters begin physically blocking the vehicle.

Protesters throw snowballs and other objects at the vehicle.

The windshield gets cracked.

The back window gets broken.

EZ-17 and EZ-2 physically push the protesters blocking the truck out of the way.

EZ-2 also deploys what appears to be a canister of OC spray.

A person begins banging on the windows of the truck.

EZ-17 rushes around the truck to fire his launcher towards this person’s face.

Chemical irritant smoke was seen being released by the projectiles from this last shot as it travelled through the air.

The multiple projectiles are consistent with the 40mm “SKAT Shell” by Defense Technology.

The 40mm “SKAT Shell” ejects four separate submunitions upon firing, each dispensing chemical irritants.

In one of the videos, a SKAT Shell is seen in EZ-17’s belt.

Children in Chicago’s Old Irving Park neighbourhood were preparing for a Halloween parade on Oct. 25 when federal agents reportedly deployed tear gas on the street to disperse protesters opposing immigration-related arrests in the neighbourhood.

US District Judge Sara Ellis said in court on Tuesday, according to a CBS News report: “Those kids were tear gassed on their way to celebrate Halloween in their local school parking lot,” and “I can only imagine how terrifi ed they were.”

Ellis was questioning US Customs and Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino over incidents that protesters allege violate a temporary restraining order (TRO) she issued earlier this month.

The Oct. 9 TRO was issued after a group of journalists, faith leaders and protesters filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration.

The lawsuit described a “pattern of extreme brutality” by federal agents against peaceful protesters since Operation Midway Blitz began on Sept. 2.

Operation Midway Blitz is described as a multi-agency operation against “criminal illegal aliens” in Illinois.

A subsequent court filing on Oct. 27 alleges that federal agents have violated the TRO “almost every day” since it was issued.

The filing stated: “Immigration enforcement does not typically require the daily use of tear gas on civilians in residential areas.”

Bellingcat’s analysis of social media videos from 28 events in Illinois from Oct. 9 to Oct. 27 found multiple examples of force and riot control weapons being used.

Seven events appeared to show the use of riot control weapons when there was seemingly no apparent immediate threat by protesters and no audible warnings given.

Nineteen events showed use of force, such as tackling people to the ground when they were not visibly resisting.

Another seven events showed agents ordering or threatening people to leave public places.

Each of the events included in the dataset were verified to have taken place in Illinois in recent weeks with at least two sources.

The sources included videos taken by different people, local reporting, or statements from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The DHS oversees Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) and the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said DHS officers “only use crowd control methods as a last resort when repeated warnings have been given”.

DHS said its officers were “facing a 1,000 percent increase in assaults against them”.

The court order places restrictions on federal agents’ crowd-control measures within the state.

The court order includes “riot control weapons” such as tear gas and pepper spray.

The court order restricts the use of force against individuals.

The court order restricts requiring people to leave public spaces that they lawfully have the right to be in.

The TRO says riot control weapons or force may be deployed where there is an “immediate threat” of physical harm to the agents or others.

The TRO says riot control weapons or force may be deployed when multiple warnings have been given.

The TRO says riot control weapons or force may be deployed where “necessary and proportional” for an arrest.

The TRO prohibits the use of riot control weapons on people “who are not posing an immediate threat to the safety of a law enforcement off icer or others”.

The TRO prohibits using riot control weapons where using them on intended targets would result in injury to others who are not posing any threat.

The TRO prohibits federal agents from “issuing a crowd dispersal order requiring any person to leave a public place that they lawfully have a right to be, unless dispersal is justifi ed by exigent circumstances as defi ned by Department of Homeland Security Use of Force Policy”.

One video captured the moment Bovino threw what looked like a tear gas canister during the Oct. 23 clashes in the Little Village neighbourhood.

The Oct. 23 clashes in Little Village were during an operation where eight people were arrested.

One of the eight people arrested was a 16-year-old US citizen.

DHS and Bovino said he was hit on the head by objects thrown by protesters before he threw the tear gas canister.

DHS posted a video on Facebook claiming that it was evidence that “the use of chemical munitions was conducted in full accordance with CBP policy and was necessary to ensure the safety of both law enforcement and the public”.

The video showed a rock skidding on the ground behind Bovino.

The video did not show the moment that the rock allegedly hit Bovino on the head.

A protester who filmed the encounter has reportedly disputed that Bovino was hit.

Tear gas was also deployed on Oct. 12 in Albany Park.

Tear gas was deployed on Oct. 14 in the East Side of Chicago.

Tear gas was deployed on Oct. 24 in Lakeview.

Tear gas was deployed on Oct. 25 in Avondale.

Bellingcat reviewed footage of each of those incidents and could not see threats to the agents’ safety before tear gas was deployed.

Bellingcat reviewed footage of each of those incidents and could not see audible warnings within the footage.

A video from the Oct. 23 protests in Little Village, posted by a protester named Enrique Bahena, shows an agent shooting a less-lethal projectile directly at the person filming.

An Oct. 26 court filing said Bahena was shot in the “neck from fi ve feet away with a pepper ball”.

Bellingcat’s analysis of the video found that the video shows the agent deploying a B&T GL-06 40mm launcher.

The B&T GL-06 40mm launcher can be used to launch chemical irritant rounds such as the one visible in the video.

Bahena said in an interview with local outlet Chicago Block Club that agents did not give warnings before they shot him “in the throat” and threw gas canisters at the group of protesters who were shouting at them to leave.

Bahena said protesters did throw objects at agents, but that was after agents had already used force.

B&T technical specifications for their 40mm projectiles state that “shots to the head, neck, spine, or heart are to be avoided unless lethal force is justified”.

B&T technical specifications advise users to aim at the waistline.

A DHS Office of Inspector General Report in 2021 states that “ICE’s use of force policy indicates that the 40MM launcher is deadly force when fired at someone, while the CBP use of force policy only directs officers not to target a person’s head or neck”.

Another video from the Oct. 23 protests in Little Village shows other officers appearing to fire less-lethal weapons towards protestors.

The TRO restricts the use of Compressed Air Launchers or Munitions Launchers such as 40mm launchers to strike a person, including on the neck, unless they pose an “immediate threat of causing serious bodily injury or death”.

In another incident on Oct. 22, an agent appeared to quickly roll down a window and spray what appeared to be a chemical irritant at protesters near a Sam’s Club store in the Cicero neighbourhood of Chicago.

The incident was captured in two separate livestreams.

The video appears to show agents dragging the driver out by her legs.

Federal agents have frequently used so-called “less-lethal” weapons against protesters, including impact projectiles, tear gas and pepper spray, since the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration raids began last year.

The use of less-lethal weapons (LLWs) has been controversial.

LLWs are designed to incapacitate or control a person without causing death or permanent injury.

LLWs can cause serious or fatal injuries, especially when used improperly.

Earlier this month, two protesters in California were reportedly blinded after US federal agents fired less-lethal rounds at their faces from close range.

These incidents were part of a wave of violent clashes between agents from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and protesters across the country after the deadly shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in Minneapolis.

In protests in Minneapolis immediately following Good’s death, one Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) officer was captured on camera firing a 40mm less-lethal launcher five times in less than five minutes.

Several of these shots appeared to target protesters’ faces.

Targeting protesters’ faces is against CBP’s own use-of-force policy.

A Bellingcat investigation of DHS incidents in October 2025 also found about 30 incidents that appeared to violate a temporary restraining order (TRO) issued by an Illinois judge restricting how DHS agents could use LLWs.

It is not always obvious whether the use of a LLW is authorised or not.

DHS component agencies such as ICE and CBP have varying guidance on factors such as the level of resistance an individual needs to show before a certain type of force can be used.

DHS component agencies such as ICE and CBP have varying guidance on how specific types of less-lethal weapons and munitions can be used.

While CBP’s use-of-force policy as of January 2021 is available on its website, ICE does not include specific guidance on less-lethal weapons in its 2023 “Firearms and Use of Force” Directive.

ICE does not appear to have any publicly available policy that outlines this guidance.

DHS did not respond by publication time to Bellingcat’s request for the most recent DHS, CBP and ICE use-of-force policies.

DHS did not respond by publication time to questions about what less-lethal weapons were authorised for use by the department and its component agencies.

The DHS use-of-force policy, updated in February 2023, states that the department’s law enforcement officers and agents may use force, including LLWs, “only when no reasonably effective, safe and feasible alternative appears to exist”.

The DHS use-of-force policy says agents may only use a level of force that is “objectively reasonable in light of the facts and circumstances” that they face at the time.

DHS has repeatedly defended its use of riot-control weapons in protests across the country.

DHS stated that it was “taking reasonable and constitutional measures to uphold the rule of law and protect [its] officers”.

Compressed air, or pneumatic launchers, are essentially paintball guns that fire 0.68mm balls which break on impact.

Compressed air launchers often release a powdered chemical irritant such as oleoresin capsicum (OC) or PavaPowder.

Oleoresin capsicum (OC) and PavaPowder are the same compounds typically found in pepper spray.

Compressed air launchers can also be used with “marking” projectiles that use paint to mark an individual for later arrest.

Compressed air launchers can also be used with projectiles intended to break glass.

These weapons are often referred to as “PepperBall” guns.

The leading brand is PepperBall.

DHS agents have also been seen carrying compressed air launchers from different brands, such as the FN303, produced by FN America.

Many compressed air launchers resemble standard paintball guns, with a distinct hopper or loader mounted to the top.

Many compressed air launchers have a compressed air tank that might be mounted to the side, bottom, or inside the buttstock.

Many compressed air launchers, and less-lethal weapons in general, have very bright colours such as orange to distinguish them from lethal weapons.

The TAC-SF PepperBall gun features a compressed air tank and a top-mounted EL-2 hopper.

The PepperBall TAC-SA Pro’s hopper is a slightly different shape from the TAC-SF, but serves the same purpose.

PepperBall VKS Pro features a compressed air tank located inside the buttstock and a magazine rather than a top-mounted hopper.

Federal agents have been seen carrying FN303 compressed air launchers in videos of immigration enforcement activities.

The FN303 may resemble a rifle or other firearm.

The FN303 is usually all-black.

The FN303 lacks a visible hopper.

If closer examination is possible, the FN303 can be identified by its distinct features, including a circular magazine, side-mounted compressed air tank and a hose connecting the firearm to the air tank.

The FN303’s air tank is mounted on the side and connected to the firearm by a hose.

Compressed air launchers should not be used against small children.

Compressed air launchers should not be used against the elderly.

Compressed air launchers should not be used against visibly pregnant women.

Compressed air launchers should not be used against people operating a vehicle.

PepperBall guns should not be used within 3 feet “unless the use of deadly force is reasonable and necessary”.

When using the FN303, the minimum distance is increased to 10 feet.

The CBP Use of Force Policy says the intentional targeting of areas where there is a “substantial risk of serious bodily injury or death is considered a use of deadly force.”

Agents are instructed not to target “the head, neck, spine, or groin of the intended subject, unless the use of deadly force is reasonable”.

PepperBall and FN America provide similar warnings about avoiding vital areas to prevent serious injury or death.

According to a 2021 report by the US Office of Inspector General, ICE does not require yearly recertification to use PepperBall guns and FN303s.

40mm launchers resemble military grenade launchers.

40mm launchers are used to fire less-lethal ammunition.

40mm launchers can fire “sponge” rounds that can disperse chemical irritants on impact.

Federal agents have been seen using or carrying the B&T GL06 launcher in footage of multiple incidents reviewed by Bellingcat.

Some 40mm munitions’ primary function is chemical irritants.

Some 40mm munitions’ primary function is a combination of impact and chemical irritants.

Different types of streams increase or decrease the range of the spray.

On June 6, 2025, demonstrators began to assemble outside of the Metropolitan Detention Center in Los Angeles in response to accelerated federal raids targeting suspected undocumented immigrants.

The June 6, 2025 assembly catalyzed a series of mass protests across the country to denounce U.S. immigration policy.

This visual investigation spotlights three novel weapons.

The three weapons are scattershot impact projectiles, powder blast dispersion rounds, and chemical obscurants.

The analysis covers immigration protests from June 2025 to the present.

Scattershot impact projectiles used by the Los Angeles Police Department are described as tools of collective punishment on assemblies rarely seen in the United States.

Scattershot impact projectiles can be directly linked to the nearly 100 journalists shot with less-lethal weapons during the anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles from the summer of 2025.

Powder blast dispersion rounds are often referred to by the trade name “Muzzle Blast” rounds.

Powder blast dispersion rounds were once largely confined to correctional facilities.

Powder blast dispersion rounds have recently been used by the United States Border Patrol on the streets.

Video footage shows powder blast dispersion rounds being direct fired at protesters’ faces at very close range.

On October 23, 2025, Reverend Jorge Bautista was shot with a 40mm grenade launcher at a protest in Oakland, California.

Images from the October 23, 2025 incident show the pastor enveloped in a cloud of orange smoke after a USBP agent shot at his face from about three feet away.

A solid projectile is seen ricocheting after apparently striking Bautista in the chin.

Some speculated Bautista was shot with a “Pepperball” round.

On January 21, 2026, at Bryant Square Park in Minneapolis, a group of USBP agents was seen deploying grenades that emitted clouds of bright green smoke at protesters.

One video captured a man saying to bystanders, “the green stuff is super carcinogenic.”

Chemical obscurants are more commonly known as “smoke grenades.”

The use of chemical obscurants has a widespread misinformation problem about both identification and health impacts.

Manufacturers advertise obscurants on the civilian market as aids to crowd-control.

Manufacturers also advertise obscurants to intimidate through the psychological effect of smoke or to allegedly heighten the negative effects of tear gas.

Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) is the report author.

Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) conducted a visual investigation.

Rohini J. Haar, MD, MPH is listed as Medical Advisor.

Scott Reynhout, PhD is listed as Expert, Crowd-Control Weapons.

The report says scattershot impact projectiles are designed to spread out to hit as many people as possible.

The report says scattershot KIPs are inherently indiscriminate.

The report says most KIPs used for crowd-control in the United States are “target-specific”.

The report says scattershot KIPs are largely restricted domestically to correctional facilities, not protests.

The report says the LAPD is unique in the United States for its extensive use of scattershot KIPs for crowd-control.

The report says the LAPD’s continued use of technology unsuited for crowd-control creates an unusually hazardous protest environment.

The report says powder blast dispersion rounds are not technically a projectile.

The report says powder blast dispersion rounds can extend up to 30 feet in front of the shooter.

The report says powder blast dispersion rounds carry serious health risks when fired at close ranges.

The report says close-range use has resulted in facial, eye and neck injuries from the wadding and other traumatic impacts.

The report says the USBP appears to favor powder blast for crowd-control.

The report says the USBP procurement document covered five varieties for “Crowd Management” and $50 million worth of less-lethal specialty munitions.

The report says the use of powder blast dispersion weapons at close range defies both convention and practical assessments of risk.

The report says the pattern of use adds to demonstrably unsafe uses of crowd-control weapons since 2025.

The report says chemical obscurants can be toxic, carcinogenic, and arguably more dangerous than common chemical irritants.

The report says the confusion of obscurants with far more hazardous substances contributes to an environment of fear.

The report says the lack of regulations around smoke obscurants in the United States allows for potentially unlimited use and potential abuse.

The report says the First Amendment affirms the right to peaceful assembly, extending to peaceful protest.

The report says the Fourth Amendment is the standard for evaluating law enforcement’s use of force through whether the officer’s use of force was objectively reasonable.

The report quotes Graham v. Connor factors as (1) “the severity of the crime at issue,” (2) “whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of the officers or others,” and (3) whether the suspect “is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight.”

The report says UN Guidance section 7.3.6 treats shots to the head as unlawful.

The report says UN Guidance section 7.2.3 supports additional testing to evaluate toxicological evidence of the hazards of aerosolized chemical cocktails.

The report says UN Guidance section 7.2.5 deems HC smoke unfit for use in crowd-control.

The report says the UN Chemical Weapons Convention defines permitted riot control agents as having transient effects that “disappear within a short time following termination of exposure,” and not causing any significant long term injuries.

The report says HC smoke does not fall under that definition.

The report says CCWs should be designed to be proportional and discriminate while aiming to minimize harm.

The report says all safety datasheets and relevant health-risk information must be publicly accessible by weapons producers.

The report says state actors must ensure CCWs are subject to strict independent testing.

The report says law enforcement officials should record and report the model of CCW deployed, distance from the target, duration of deployment, the number of CCWs of each type used, and documented or reported injuries.

The report says all cases of deaths, injuries, and suspected misuse of CCWs should be investigated by an entity independent of the unit or department involved.

The report says responsible officers and their commanders should be held liable and subject to administrative disciplinary measures and/or criminal prosecution in the event of unlawful conduct.

The report says “Less-lethal” crowd-control weapons when misused can cause serious injury, disability, and death.
